Constant plumbing backups are frustrating enough on their own. But when the problem keeps coming back, and the source is hiding somewhere along a long sewer line, figuring out what’s actually happening inside the pipe can be the hardest part.

That’s where a sewer inspection camera can help. Instead of just guessing, plumbers, drain-cleaning technicians and experienced property owners can visually inspect accessible portions of a line for signs of root intrusion, buildup, standing water, cracks, offsets and other visible problems before deciding what comes next.

The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is designed for those longer, more demanding inspections. A rigid push cable, self-leveling camera and bright adjustable lighting help operators work farther into sewer lines while recording what they find along the way.

The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is a professional-grade pipe inspection system built to provide a clear view inside longer drain and sewer lines.

One of its most notable features is the 9-millimeter rigid push cable, available in 165-, 230- or 328-foot lengths. The added stiffness gives you the pushing support needed to move the camera through longer pipe runs, although actual reach will depend on the diameter, bends, layout and condition of the line.

Industry observers note that at the end of the cable is a 31-millimeter self-leveling camera head. The self-leveling design keeps the image upright as the camera rotates inside the pipe, making footage easier to interpret than video that constantly spins as the cable moves.

Visibility is another priority. The camera head is covered with 24 LEDs with five levels of adjustable brightness. You can adjust the brightness to get a better look at roots, debris, buildup, cracks and other visible pipe conditions in otherwise completely dark lines.

Sources indicate that the video footage is displayed on a 9-inch IPS monitor at AHD 1080P resolution. Photos, video and audio can also be recorded to the memory card (included), making it easier to review an inspection later, document a problem or show a customer or plumbing professional exactly what was found.

For recurring problems, that documentation can be particularly useful. Rather than simply knowing that a line is backing up, an inspection can help establish whether there is a visible obstruction, root intrusion or pipe damage that may require cleaning or repair.

The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera houses its inspection equipment in a wheeled system that moves effortlessly between jobs while keeping cables easy to manage.

Key specifications and features include:.

In a recent development, the SANYIPACE sewer camera can be used in straight pipes larger than about 1.6 inches without the guide wheel. When the included 4.25-inch guide wheel is installed, SANYIPACE recommends using it in straight pipes larger than about 4.7 inches.

It’s also worth remembering that this is an inspection tool, not a drain-cleaning tool. Once a problem is identified, the appropriate cleaning or repair method should be carried out separately.

The SANYIPACE sewer camera is best suited to professionals who regularly need to inspect longer drain and sewer lines rather than homeowners looking for a simple camera to occasionally check a sink drain.

For plumbers and drain-cleaning technicians, the combination of a rigid push cable, powerful lighting and self-leveling imaging can make it easier to assess pipe conditions before deciding whether a line needs cleaning, root removal or repair. The recording feature also provides documentation that can be reviewed later or shown directly to customers.

According to recent reports, this also makes sense for sewer inspection specialists and plumbing contractors who frequently work on longer pipe runs. With cable configurations up to 328 feet, you can choose a setup that better matches the types of jobs you typically encounter.

Another fit could be property maintenance professionals and facility maintenance teams, particularly when they are responsible for drainage systems that require recurring inspection and documentation.

It has been revealed that experienced homeowners and hands-on property owners may also find this to be a useful tool when dealing with a long sewer line or a recurring drainage problem. In those situations, being able to document what is visible inside the pipe can make conversations with a plumber considerably more productive. However, diagnosing what the footage means (as well as determining the safest repair) may still require a plumbing professional.

In a recent development, the SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is available directly from SANYIPACE in several cable-length and locator configurations. As of press time, the 165-foot version without a locator is listed for $1,799.99. Pricing increases with longer cable lengths and configurations that include a compatible locator. Family Handyman readers can save an additional $100 with code FH100 at checkout.

If long sewer runs are a regular part of your work, this sewer camera offers the core features that matter most for inspection—such as pushability, adjustable brightness, upright imaging and recording—in a single transportable system.

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Staying properly hydrated has many health benefits—it promotes cardiovascular health, enhances skin elasticity, and eliminates waste from the body—and using a countertop water filter is an easy way to get safe, clean drinking water right in your kitchen. These user-friendly appliances either sit on your counter or attach to your faucet, removing common contaminants like chemicals, heavy metals, and bacteria without requiring permanent plumbing. Not only that, they help reduce the plastic waste associated with buying bottled water.

To help you find the right one for your water quality and household needs, we spent 2 weeks testing seven of the most popular models on the market today. Based on our results, we chose the Bluevua Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter System as our favorite for its easy setup, third-party contaminant removal certifications, long filter life, and remineralization stage that restores beneficial minerals for a smooth taste. Read on for our detailed reviews of the best countertop water filters and to learn what matters most when choosing the one for you.

Bottom line: Countertop water filters offer a convenient way to access clean, safe drinking water, with options to suit various needs and budgets.

Recent findings suggest that the products below represent the “best in show” in home water filtration. These top picks were chosen based on quality, functionality, and reputation.

Sources indicate that this was the first unit we tested, and it ended up being our favorite. Installation was incredibly easy—just fill the removable water reservoir, plug the unit in, and press start. As with any reverse osmosis (RO) water filter system, you’ll also want to discard the first two tanks of water as part of flushing the new filters, but after that, you’ll get nothing but pure, great-tasting water. In fact, we thought the water from this model was some of the best, due to its comprehensive filtration as well as the fact that it undergoes a remineralization stage to add calcium and magnesium back in for a super smooth taste.

Sources indicate that another favorite feature was the built-in LCD screen that shows total dissolved solids (TDS) before and after each cycle, giving us visible proof that its NSF- and WQA-certified filtration system was actively removing contaminants. That display also shows when it’s time to replace each of the four filters (they all have relatively long lifespans of 12 to 24 months), and changing them is easy since they twist right out (there’s also a reset button for each one to update its filter life indicator). We also really liked that it dispenses directly into a glass carafe that maintains the water’s crisp taste and fits easily into our fridge. The Bluevua isn’t the least expensive model on this list, but for an RO unit with remineralization, it provides an excellent value—provided you have the counter space for it.

Industry observers note that what our tester says: “I’ve been drinking alkaline water for years, and I greatly prefer it to the flat taste of reverse osmosis water. Since the Bluevua gives me both, it’s my new favorite water filter!”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Like the Bluevua, it features a digital display that shows TDS levels before and after filtration, and like every unit we tested, it passed our manual water-quality tests with flying colors.

While traditional RO systems can be a bit of a pain to install, setting up this countertop reverse osmosis filter is as easy as plugging it in, filling the reservoir, and throwing away the first couple of pitchers. You can filter water directly into your own container or the included 32-ounce water tank, which means you can chill one batch in the fridge while still having the option to grab a quick room-temp cup. The tech giant consistently prioritizes user-friendliness, and because this RO model also adds minerals back in, the final product tastes excellent.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer.

If you want reliable multi-stage water filtration without giving up counter space or worrying about cords, this simple pitcher filter from Epic could be ideal. The simple gravity-fed setup is compact enough for small apartments and dorm rooms and user-friendly enough for anyone seeking straightforward pour-in, pour-out convenience. Despite its small footprint, it offers as much or more capacity than many options on this list, storing easily on the counter or in the fridge.

According to recent reports, setting up the Waterdrop M6CG couldn’t have been much easier. After filling the rear reservoir and getting everything running, we were impressed by how neatly the unit fit into a coffee and tea station despite giving you both hot and cold filtered water. We initially wished there was an option to connect it directly to a water line, but since an RO system also needs somewhere to send wastewater, the refillable tank setup will probably be more practical for most kitchens anyway. Most importantly, the filtered water tasted noticeably better than our unfiltered tap water, and the hot-water function gave us water that was more than hot enough for tea without waiting for a kettle.

Compared with a refrigerator dispenser or traditional water cooler, the Waterdrop feels extremely slow, particularly when filling a mug with hot water. It has been revealed that we also liked the glass carafe attached to the machine, which fills from the bottom and keeps room-temperature filtered water ready to grab at any time (it also looks and feels super premium). The system provides helpful reminders when the reservoir needs attention, although they can occasionally feel unnecessary, such as reminding us to refill or empty the tank while we’re already removing it to do exactly that. Overall, this is a capable, attractive RO dispenser that produces great-tasting water and useful hot and cold options. We just wish its dispensing speed and interface felt a little more polished given the premium price.

Comparing the certifications of all the filtered water systems in this guide had its confusing moments, but as we worked, we learned that the AquaTru Classic RO system is one of the most highly certified units on the market. With its comprehensive four-stage design, it can trap a total of 84 contaminants, including everything from coarse sediment and chlorine to heavy metals, fluoride, microplastics, and forever chemicals (PFAS). And with a 2.84-liter clean water tank, it also holds more purified water than any other reverse osmosis system on our list.

Because the filters last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years (depending on which of the three filters you’re replacing), maintenance is also minimal, especially compared to standard pitcher filters. Like all RO systems, though, it also takes up more counter space than basic units. Ultimately, its higher upfront cost and lack of remineralization kept it out of the top spot, but those with high-capacity demands who love everything else about it will be happy to hear AquaTru sells replacement filters with minerals—making cost the only real hurdle.

Get the AquaTru countertop water filter at Amazon, The Home Depot, Best Buy, or AquaTru.

One of the biggest downsides of faucet-connected systems is that their hoses can easily get in the way of other sink-related tasks, like washing your hands or doing the dishes. They also create a cluttered look, which Brondell seems to acknowledge, as the brand doesn’t show any photos of this model actually hooked up to a faucet. However, if you purchase an inexpensive T-valve and don’t mind drilling a small hole in your countertop, you can run that hose under your sink for a totally seamless look. And because this pick allows for virtually instant filtration, you get purified water on demand no matter which setup you choose.

Industry observers note that performance-wise, the Cypress countertop filter uses a three-stage system that combines a sediment filter, a patented Nanotrap filter, and a carbon block to pull out chlorine, microplastics, VOCs, and fine particles. Water dispenses instantly at the press of a button with zero wastewater generated, making it faster than gravity pitchers and more efficient than reverse osmosis setups. It also has a slim footprint that takes up minimal countertop space, though because it’s only about 10 inches tall, it’s hard to fill tall bottles or large pots (we had to reposition it over the sink to do so during testing). Still, it comes at a great price for a WQA Gold Seal-certified unit with filters that last 6 months to 1 year, making it a good water filter for homes with high-volume needs.

Get the Brondell countertop water filter at Amazon or Brondell.

There’s no denying the popularity of the Significant Berkey: its stainless steel construction and massive 8.5-liter capacity have made it a staple for large households and off-grid enthusiasts. Because it relies strictly on gravity and its proprietary Black Berkey filters, it functions entirely without electricity, plumbing, or tap pressure—you simply pour water into the top chamber and let it drip down. It also has an extremely long filter lifespan of up to 6,000 gallons per pair, meaning you won’t be constantly buying replacements.

According to recent reports, however, its popularity comes with a couple of drawbacks. Despite the hefty price tag, Berkey lacks any official certifications, relying instead on independent lab testing. And like all gravity systems, it’s also quite bulky, standing almost 20 inches tall with no option for fridge storage. Also, because it relies on gravity, the filtration rate is quite slow—we got into the habit of filling the top reservoir a couple of times a day so it had several hours to make its way to the bottom. Still, with no gauge of any sort, we never really had any idea how much water was even in the bottom chamber. All that aside, Berkey has an almost cult-like following, and the durable stainless steel water filter body and straightforward operation are likely why.

Get the Massive Berkey countertop water filter at Amazon.

To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

According to recent reports, after selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

It has been revealed that the best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

Countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

Sources indicate that reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Big Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Recent findings suggest that faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

Recent findings suggest that two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more important to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

It has been revealed that most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

According to recent reports, many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

According to recent reports, then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

Capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

Recent findings suggest that flow rate—how quickly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another important consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

Every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

Water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

No, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

According to recent reports, most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Industry observers note that filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need new filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

According to recent reports, the Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

It depends. Salting before a major storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

According to recent reports, proposal to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

It’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

The best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, claims.

Apply salt before and after a big storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

According to recent reports, “Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, says. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

If only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

Recent findings suggest that “The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how significant the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski claims. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland claims. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

Rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski says. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

In a recent development, yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

“While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski says.

There’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

Industry observers note that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s important to solidify your shoveling proposal before the first snow flies.

“Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”.

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

Industry observers note that shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” claims grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

To make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” says Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”.

A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” says Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”.

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aliaksandr Bahdanovich/Getty Images.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” claims Flores.

In a recent development, the fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, says Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, claims Lopez.

According to recent reports, just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

“Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” notes Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”.

In a recent development, A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

“Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” says Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

After a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

Pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” says Lopez. “.

Try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

“Before winter arrives, strategy where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” states Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”.

Also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

Aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

Industry observers note that safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” notes Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural matter.”.

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

Recent findings suggest that to stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” says Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”.

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” says Schwab.

According to recent reports, sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

It has been revealed that “Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” says Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”.

In a recent development, obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

Start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” states Flores.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.

It has been revealed that [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed newly introduced limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing fresh terms for future cooperation in any event….

In a recent development, [But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a newly introduced state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "problem orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

It has been revealed that our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

According to recent reports, we also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

It has been revealed that judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

In a recent development, electrical tape comes in plenty of colors, but each has a purpose. Here's what the common shades mean in U.S. electrical work.

Being a DIY electrician is one way homeowners like to save a little money over expensive repairs. However, there are safety concerns when it comes to doing your own electrical work. Electrical tape color meanings help electricians identify wires and make sense of connections that might otherwise look identical. The trouble is that colors don’t always mean the same thing.

Learn what the common colors usually mean, how electricians use them, and why a strip of tape can’t confirm a wire’s purpose.

In a recent development, electricians use colored tape to identify wires, especially when several look alike. In the United States, the colors commonly mean:.

These colors aren’t universal. The National Electrical Code sets rules for identifying neutral and grounding wires, but most hot-wire colors follow common practices rather than strict requirements. For example, orange can have a specific meaning in certain commercial electrical systems. Its purpose depends on the wiring, so electricians can’t rely on color alone.

Electricians often wrap colored tape around the ends of wires to tell them apart. Manufacturers such as 3M make tape specifically for identifying different electrical connections.

Tape can also show when a wire serves a different purpose than its original color suggests. For example, electricians may mark a white wire with black tape to identify it as a hot wire in certain situations. Electrical codes limit when and how they can make these changes.

However, tape color alone can’t confirm a wire’s purpose or whether it carries electricity. Previous repairs, incorrect markings, or different labeling practices can cause confusion. Before starting electrical work, a qualified person should identify the circuit and test that the power is off. Homeowners who encounter unfamiliar or conflicting wire markings should have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring.

But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

Absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

According to recent reports, there is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

Behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

One feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

The Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

Recent findings suggest that it’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

According to recent reports, another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

Industry observers note that my only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a new prescription for glasses.

At $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

Dupray advertises coverage up to 1,517 square feet, but that’s based on just one air change per hour. For more frequent air cleaning, it’s rated to cover 316 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. I’d use that smaller figure when choosing where to place it.

The Bloom also offers an optional wood tabletop model for anyone who prefers an accent table instead of a planter.

I love having a living plant incorporated into an appliance I’d otherwise try to hide. The Bloom is one of the few air purifiers I’ve tested that I’d happily put on display.

What It Really Means When Your Mayor Awards Someone the “Key to the City”

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause.
  • Cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors. Here's why cities give them out and what recipients actually receive.

Whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause. But what does the key actually do?

Cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize. Learn what a key to the city represents, how the custom began, and what someone actually gets to do with it.

A key to the city is an award that cities give to people they want to honor.

“The Key to the City is presented as a symbol of civic recognition and Philadelphia’s appreciation for individuals whose achievements, service and influence have made a meaningful impact on the city and its people,” according to a release from the City of Philadelphia.

According to recent reports, the key is usually decorative, with the city’s name or seal on it. Some come in a display box or with a certificate. Little Rock, Arkansas, considers its key the city’s highest ceremonial honor.

It has been revealed that but the key won’t open City Hall or any other public building. It doesn’t give the recipient special privileges or any authority, either. In 2010, Newly introduced York City tried something different with an art project that gave people working keys to certain locations. Those weren’t the same as the city’s usual honorary keys.

The tradition goes back to when cities had walls and gates that closed at night. Giving someone a key meant they could come and go without asking permission.

In a recent development, in medieval Europe, leaders also exchanged keys during official visits or military surrenders. Handing over the keys sometimes meant giving up control of a city. Over time, the custom became a way to welcome or honor someone.

Today, cities give keys to athletes, public figures, volunteers, and local residents. Each city has its own rules for who receives one.

Philadelphia, for example, honored a resident in 2026 after he walked across the country to support career opportunities for young people. Elk Grove, California, recognizes military accomplishments and acts of heroism, while Little Rock reserves its keys for people who live outside Arkansas.

Mayors usually present the keys, although some cities involve the city council or accept nominations from residents. Recipients get a keepsake and some public recognition, but no special privileges.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

From a surprising way to monitor power outages to an epic trick to double your Ziploc bags, Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

According to recent reports, “The metal wheels of a refrigerator can scratch, dent or gouge just about any flooring surface. Laying down stiff cardboard or a piece of leftover carpet provides an effective barrier, but for the best protection, use a sheet of 1/8‑in. hardboard. The smooth surface protects floors and helps appliances slide into and out of place. —ANTHONY LOMBARDI.

“To find out if power outages ruined the food in your freezer while you were away on vacation, freeze a container of water and rest a penny on top of the ice. If the penny is at the bottom when you get back, it means the power was off long enough to melt the water—as well as thaw (and likely spoil) everything in the freezer. —JOHN NAKAMURA.

Dan Roberts for Family Handyman.

“If you don’t have a label handy, use a rubber band instead. Stretch it around your Mason jar, then write the contents with a permanent marker. The grippy rubber also makes the jar easier to open. —DAVID KOWALCZYK Picture Frame Message Board I wanted a nicer-looking place for my weekly grocery list and family notes, so I turned a picture frame into a dry-erase board. I simply cut decorative paper to fit the frame and put it behind the glass, creating a surface I can write on with a dryerase marker. —JESSIE DAWSON.

“For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD.

Recent findings suggest that “Leaky seals around faucets and sink rims can lead to slow but severe damage (they can destroy a countertop, for example). So after installing a new sink or faucet, dribble water around the area and wait a few minutes. Then get under the sink and look for leaks. —GREGORY PRITCHARD.

Sources indicate that “Sometimes it’s tough to mix foods such as old-fashioned oily peanut butter in a small jar by hand. But if you enjoy reaching for a power tool to solve a problem as I do, head out to the garage. As it turns out, the handle of a mixing spoon fits perfectly in the chuck of a cordless drill. —CLIFF MERCER.

“Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. Screw a floor flange to the cabinet, thread in a 3-in.-long pipe nipple, and then thread a 90-degree elbow onto the nipple. Cut the vertical pipe so it’s a bit longer than the width of the roll of bags. Finally, thread the vertical piece into the elbow and slip on the roll.” —TRAVIS LARSON.

Industry observers note that “I turn sandwich-size bags into snack-size bags by heating up an old butter knife with a lighter and slicing the bag in half. The hot knife cauterizes the edges of the two fresh bags, and the cauterized edges are just as strong as the factory-sealed edges.” —JULIA TRENTON.

According to recent reports, “Need to sharpen a utility knife, pocket blade or scissors but don’t have a sharpening stone on hand? Flip a ceramic mug and use the unglazed ring on the bottom as a sharpener. Hold the blade at a 45-degree angle and slide it across the ring in one direction, from the base to the tip. This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can rapidly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ.

“Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. I like to keep several on hand to use in lunches and coolers, as well as for first aid. They’re inexpensive to make, easy to reuse and help reduce waste.” —TOM SHERIDAN.

Emiko Franzen for Family Handyman.

“Alphabetizing spices helps you quickly find what your recipe calls for and makes putting away jars just as fast. Another benefit? You can easily figure out which spices are missing from your pantry, so you’re less likely to discover you’re out of a key ingredient halfway through making a meal. Take a quick glance before grocery shopping to keep staples stocked.” —MARTIN SUTHERLAND.

“When your favorite candle burns too low for a lighter or match to reach the wick, don’t risk burning your fingertips. Instead, light a piece of uncooked spaghetti. It is long enough to reach deep into tall candle holders and burns long enough to light the wick.” —PATRICIA HART.

According to recent reports, “For an extra-fresh garbage disposal, toss in a few lemon or lime peels. Run the disposal with cold water until you can’t hear any more grinding, then run it for another 30 seconds (with the water still on).” —GREGORY HOLT.

“A countertop isn’t the best place to keep a recipe while you’re cooking. It takes up counter space, is difficult to read and is bound to get splattered. Instead, use a clothes hanger with pants clips to hang the recipe from a cabinet handle. Open the book or magazine to the desired page (or use a printout), clamp it in place and you have a simple hanging stand. This trick works best with smaller cookbooks, magazines or single-sheet recipes.” —GLENN WHITE.

In a recent development, “My kitchen drawers used to be an absolute wreck, with pans and dishes crammed in however they’d fit. And seemingly every time I needed something, it was at the very bottom of the drawer. My solution was to cut a piece of 1/8-in. pegboard to the size of the drawer bottom and attach dowels using screws from underneath. Now my pans are organized and easy to access. The 10 minutes it took to build was easily made up with how much frustration it has saved me.” —JIM DAVIDSON.

“Crawling under a kitchen sink to refill the soap dispenser was a hassle, so I tried filling it from above. But when I did, the soap formed an air-lock bubble and overflowed, creating a mess. That’s when I came up with the idea of inserting a drinking straw in the dispenser neck to relieve “bubble block.” Now when I refill the dispenser, the air escapes through the straw and the soap stays where it belongs.” —PAUL SNYDER.

In a recent development, “A dishwasher makes quick work of disinfecting washable toys such as plastic building blocks. Drop the blocks in a mesh laundry bag and run your dishwasher as usual. Remove the bag before the drying cycle, letting the blocks air-dry on a towel. This method also works for items such as seashells, dish brushes, sponges and rags.” —ROBERT VALENTI.

“If your refrigerator stops dispensing water after you change the filter, make sure the upcoming filter is fully seated. Many people don’t twist it in completely, and one final turn may be all it takes to get the dispenser working again.” —STANLEY BEAUMONT.

Recent findings suggest that “An ironing board with the cover removed can be used as an extra cooling rack when you’re doing a lot of baking. Better yet, it frees up valuable counter space for other kitchen tasks. Just be sure to use pans, paper liners, parchment or some other barrier between baked goods and the board.” —LIZ GRABOWSKI.

Katie Synold for Family Handyman.

Recent findings suggest that “When the rubber sink baffle on my garbage disposal gets grimy or starts to smell, I switch off the power at the breaker and scrub it with an old toothbrush dipped in hot, soapy water and baking soda. I lift the rubber flaps to clean underneath, where food and grime collect. Then I restore power, rinse it with cold water and run the disposal briefly to flush away the debris.” —CHARLES MCALLISTER.

At $2,395 for the king size I tested, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper is absolutely a luxury purchase. After sleeping on it for 2 months during a Florida summer, however, I can say that its temperature-control technology delivers. This 2-inch topper uses fans, airflow, heating elements, and temperature sensors to regulate each side of the bed independently, creating a surprisingly effective way to stay comfortable throughout the night. While some aspects of the design could use a little more refinement, the actual cooling performance left me impressed.

Installation was straightforward. I unpacked the vacuum-sealed topper, laid it over my king mattress, added my usual fitted sheet, and plugged it in. The power supply is fairly big, but I had no trouble tucking it down behind my headboard. The cables emerge from the head of the topper, which is worth keeping in mind if you tend to stretch your arms overhead while sleeping. As for comfort, the topper has an unusual feel at first—slightly firm but with enough give to stay comfortable. Its internal mesh structure allows air to circulate beneath you, and the effect is immediately noticeable, even on lower settings.

It has been revealed that the cooling performance is easily my favorite feature. Even at level 3, I could feel a gentle, pleasant stream of cool air underneath me, which was especially welcome during warm Florida nights. The one trade-off is fan noise, which becomes quite noticeable at higher settings. Anything above level 5 was too loud for my sleeping preferences, but I found an easy workaround using the app’s scheduling feature. I’d run the cooling at a higher setting for about an hour before bedtime, then lower it to level 3 when I climbed into bed. This gave me the best of both worlds: a wonderfully cool mattress at bedtime and gentle, nearly silent cooling throughout the night.

It has been revealed that there are a few areas where I’d love to see Perfectly Snug make improvements, especially considering the premium price. The power supply and small side-mounted control panel are functional but have a fairly basic appearance. I also occasionally brushed against the fans positioned at the foot of the topper, which could briefly interrupt their operation (making a noticeable “you’ve just stopped a fan from moving” type of buzzing sound). The companion app was another underwhelming aspect of the experience. While it offers useful features like scheduling and temperature adjustments, its interface feels super dated and could benefit from a much more polished, intuitive design. None of these problems prevented me from enjoying the topper, but they’re details I’d expect to see addressed at this price point.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper gets the most important thing right: keeping your bed at a comfortable temperature. I enjoyed slipping into a perfectly cooled bed each night, and the subtle airflow on lower settings noticeably improved my sleep comfort. It’s an innovative product with plenty to offer, particularly for hot sleepers or couples with different temperature preferences. Although the fan noise and a few less-refined design elements keep it from feeling like a truly premium experience, the core technology is admirable. With some thoughtful improvements, this could be an outstanding luxury sleep upgrade.

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's upcoming law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) matter:.

We vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.

According to recent reports, we conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

In a recent development, I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

The anti-mask law presents more difficult complications because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:.

At bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law. Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a latest parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

According to recent reports, parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

It has been revealed that drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

Not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”.

The benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

According to recent reports, there’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

According to recent reports, some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”.

In a recent development, back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

Latest Update: 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.
  • Sources indicate that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
  • Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Sources indicate that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Industry observers note that ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

In a recent development, de-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy claims.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Recent findings suggest that conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy states. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy claims.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher states.

In a recent development, natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Sources indicate that weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice rapidly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher indicates, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Sources indicate that regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy indicates. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.

According to recent reports, I’ve tested several Aiper cleaners over the years, and the Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra feels like a natural evolution of the brand’s previous models. I ran it through repeated cleaning cycles in my 8,500-gallon saltwater pool in Florida, where leaves, bugs, fine debris, and the occasional patch of algae give pool robots plenty to deal with. Setup was super simple: The Aiper app connected quickly, the robot updated without any fuss, and I had it in the water about 15 minutes after opening the box.

What impressed me right away was just how much the Scuba V3 Ultra can do in one cleaning cycle. Plenty of the robotic pool cleaners we’ve tested at Bob Vila handle floors, walls, and the waterline, but only a select few can also skim floating debris from the surface. That matters in my open-air pool, which regularly collects bugs and leaves. Anything the Aiper actually reaches gets cleaned extremely well.

The MicroMesh filter is another highlight. It traps extremely fine material, including algae and sediment that can slip through coarser filter baskets. Cleaning that ultra-fine layer takes a little more effort—I usually spend a few minutes thoroughly rinsing it with a hose and then leave it out to dry—but that’s a fair trade-off for how much fine material it captures. The app is also among the better pool-cleaner apps I’ve used, and I like getting a notification when the cleaning cycle is finished. The robot then floats neatly near the pool edge for retrieval.

In a recent development, where the V3 Ultra disappointed me was its claim of shallow-area cleaning. Aiper claims it can work in water down to about 7.9 inches deep, but my sun shelf is apparently too shallow for it to clean reliably. I still have to brush debris from the shelf into the main pool and let the robot collect it there. It also won’t clean my pool steps. For a $2,300 machine marketed around near-total pool coverage, those are significant omissions—especially since sun shelves have become so common in newer pools.

Still, I’m a fan of the Scuba V3 Ultra overall. My older Aiper cleaner has been running reliably for close to two years, which gives me more confidence in the brand than I’d have from a short-term test alone. The voice assistant is useful without being obnoxious, retrieval is simple, filtration is excellent, and cleaning performance everywhere the robot can reach is phenomenal. I’m still waiting for the robot that will truly clean every inch of my pool, but the Scuba V3 Ultra gets closer than most.
