#148596. Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v.
  • That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.
  • First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004. The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today.".

That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v). So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated. The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof. Second, they included certain features, including:.

a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –.

(i) a folding or telescoping stock;.

(ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;.

(iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and.

In a recent development, (v) a grenade launcher…. 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

Under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names. A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

Industry observers note that but guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip. None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design. Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock. How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount? A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could. Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

Industry observers note that and so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design. Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

According to recent reports, manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance. I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw). As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

Industry observers note that connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994. The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design. And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

Sources indicate that the business end of a floor mop is typically either disposable or reusable. Disposable options are convenient for quick touch-ups and smaller floors, while reusable ones often prove more budget-friendly and can tackle larger surfaces.

Both types of mopheads impact sustainability, but in different ways. Reusable mopheads require water and chemicals to launder after use, while disposable versions head straight to the landfill. For larger areas, a reusable, machine-washable mophead is probably more efficient and eco-friendly than using multiple disposable mopheads per cleaning session. According to recent reports, if pushing a manual mop around seems laborious and inefficient, consider an electric model. Those who still want more information on cleaning hardwood flooring with a quality mop may find it here in the answers to some of the most common questions about this household chore.

In a recent development, mopping correctly can be a great way to maintain hardwood flooring, but using the wrong cleaning products can actually damage these expensive surfaces. A damp mop is often all that’s required to clean a hardwood floor; if the mop is too wet (with water or cleaning solution), excess liquid can seep into the cracks, causing the wood to warp.

Cleaning a floor starts with removing dust and debris by sweeping, vacuuming, or dry-mopping. For stubborn dirt and stains, use a cleaner designed for the specific floor material, using a “less is more” approach according to the manufacturer’s directions. To mop a floor correctly, dip string or sponge mops in the cleaning fluid, wring it out, and then swab with the damp mop. Use plain water to do a final rinse if desired. Start mopping in a far corner of the room, moving in the direction of the grain on hardwood floors, and work your way to the door. When finished, rinse the mop and let it air dry or wash any reusable pads.

It has been revealed that swiffer’s heavy-duty pads are considered safe for linoleum, vinyl, laminate, and ceramic tile, as well as sealed wood, marble, and stone. They should not be used on unsealed wood floors. As with all floor cleaners, be cautious using any fluid on unfinished, damaged, or especially delicate materials.

The National Wood Flooring Association recommends a heavy-duty mopping on wood floors monthly with a wood-flooring cleaner. However, it is safe to dry-mop daily or do a light mop on high-traffic areas once a week. For those without children and pets, feel free to give a very light mop on light-traffic areas more often.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

In a recent development, with autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not new to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

In a recent development, shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

Industry observers note that the safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

“The most important tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer states. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

Consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

In a recent development, keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer notes. That’s why it’s notable to pace yourself, stop regularly and plan ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will swiftly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

Industry observers note that “Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer indicates. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

In a recent development, dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

According to recent reports, those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Sources indicate that drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Industry observers note that rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

Drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

In a recent development, drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

According to recent reports, more serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment. If Bowie knives in common use by law-abiding citizens may be banned, the argument goes, so too may semiautomatic rifles.

A word of caution. To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife. Knives generally have a point and an edge on one side, sometimes also an edge on the other. Any knife can be used for good or bad. Bruen distinguished heavy weapons of war like lancegays from daggers, noting that in medieval society "[a]lmost everyone carried a knife or a dagger in his belt," "[c]ivilians wore them for self-protection," and "the smaller medieval weapons … strike us as most analogous to modern handguns.".

No doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are stated to have carried them concealed. But for a variety of reasons, it's unnecessary to decide whether Bowie knives met the Heller test of being in common use. Four of the amicus briefs are right on point on this glitch: National Rifle Ass'n (NRA), National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF), Senator Ted Cruz, and the United States (U.S.).

According to recent reports, first, a few States' restrictions are not enough to establish a historical tradition. Under Heller, a handful of outlier laws cannot justify a ban. "Most States regulated Bowie knives in some manner, but, except in a few outlier jurisdictions, adults were free to buy, possess, and openly carry them. Regulations typically restricted concealed carry, sales to minors, or imposed enhanced penalties for criminal misuse." NRA Br. 5.

Second, "No State banned Bowie-knife possession in the nineteenth century." NRA Br. 36. "And one of the only laws that likely did actually ban Bowie knives (along with pistols and an array of other items) is the same 1837 Georgia law that was promptly held unconstitutional other than as applied to concealed carry—because it was too restrictive to comply with the Second Amendment. See 1837 Ga. Acts 90, §1 (1838); Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243 (1846); cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 54 (singling out Nunn as "particularly instructive" on the Second Amendment's meaning)." NSSF Br. 21.

These were concealed-carry restrictions, not complete bans. "This Court has already concluded that restrictions on concealed carry cannot justify carry bans, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 48-49, 53-55, let alone possession bans, see Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-29." NSSF Br. 21.

Third, the same laws covered handguns. "If those laws justified rifle bans, then handgun bans would be justified all the more, because they typically also regulated handguns but not long guns." NRA Br. 38.

According to recent reports, where Bowie-knife restrictions were upheld, courts applied the same standard Petitioners advance here: arms in common use for lawful purposes are protected, while weapons used only by criminals are not. As Judge Richardson's dissent in Bianchi explains, it does not matter that courts sometimes disagreed about whether Bowie knives were in fact in common use, because they were applying the same yardstick. "State courts have long applied the common-use test to judge such laws under state constitutional provisions securing the right to bear arms." U.S. Br. 12.

Sources indicate that fourth, even a court that viewed the Bowie knife as exceptionally deadly held that the right to carry it was protected. "And Texas's Cockrum v. State held a Bowie knife to be a protected arm—"[t]he right to carry a bowie-knife for lawful defense is secured, and must be admitted"— while sustaining an enhanced penalty for its abuse, treating the weapon's dangerousness as a reason to regulate its misuse, not a reason to deny that it was an arm. 24 Tex. 394, 402-403 (1859). Cockrum is the mirror image of the decision below: alleged dangerousness bore on regulation, not on coverage." Cruz Br. 18.

The historical answer to misuse was punishing criminals, not disarming law-abiding citizens.

"[T]he evil must be prevented by the penitentiary and gallows, and not by a general deprivation of a constitutional privilege." U.S. Br. 30 (quoting Wilson v. State).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today the Department of Justice confirmed coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

“The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

Industry observers note that “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” noted U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” noted FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” noted Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

Sources indicate that north Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

According to recent reports, the FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

According to recent reports, the effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

Industry observers note that separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

Recent findings suggest that efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

Just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a latest, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

Industry observers note that yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

And it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

According to recent reports, with his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

Industry observers note that next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

Look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

Sources indicate that but still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

It has been revealed that overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

What’s better than a hike through fragrant evergreens with the nip of crisp winter air (and the effort of chopping your own Christmas tree) to bring a flush to your cheeks this holiday season? Whether you’re in a forest or a tree farm, these tips will help you bring home a terrific tannenbaum.

According to recent reports, if you blueprint on heading into the woods to cut down your Christmas tree, first determine whether you need a permit to do so. Call your municipal officials, for a start. Christmas tree permits are available through Recreation.gov—but hurry, because some offices do sell out of permits.

Sources indicate that some people enjoy decking out the home for the holidays right after they’ve cleared the Thanksgiving dishes, or maybe even right after that first pumpkin spice latte of the season. But if you’re decorating a real tree, it’s best to wait. Even trees that are watered regularly get dried out within 3 weeks of cutting, so try to resist the urge to decorate too early.

Unlike the Christmas trees at the local lots, trees on a farm or in the forest don’t necessarily come in predictable 6- or 8-foot sizes. To avoid disappointment, measure the distance from floor to ceiling where you plan to place your tree to make sure you don’t cut down a tree that’s too big for your house. While you’re at it, measure the space in or above your car to make sure you’ll be able to accommodate the tree, and don’t forget to bring twine, bungees, scissors, and anything else you might need to secure the tree in (or on) your car.

According to recent reports, though cutting down your Christmas tree is a fun holiday excursion, you’ll be handling blades or saws, so it’s important to wear appropriate safety attire. Put on a pair of sturdy boots, pack a pair of heavy work gloves. Avoid wearing loose clothing to keep it from tangling in the tools or trees.

Recent findings suggest that deWalt’s 15-inch hand saw cuts on the push and pull strokes for rapid material removal, and works well at different angles. Read the review.

In a recent development, depending on where you’re cutting down your tree, there may be restrictions on the tools you can use. Although a chain saw is the quickest and easiest way to fell a tree, many tree farms and national forests don’t allow their use, so be prepared with a handsaw or axe, just in case.

In a recent development, even if you immediately spot “the one,” it’s best to do a full walk-through before you commit to a particular tree. Christmas tree farms are often arranged by size or type of tree, so taking a look at everything else that’s available will help you avoid buyer’s remorse on the way out to the car.

In a recent development, try to cut your Christmas tree as low to the ground as you possibly can. This will not only make it a taller tree, but it will also allow another tree to resprout and spread Christmas cheer to future tree-hunters.

Sources indicate that have a partner hold your tree steady to prevent it from falling over before you’ve sawed all the way through the trunk. Also, resist the temptation to push the tree over: Not only is this unsafe, but it will also prevent regrowth.

Your freshly cut Christmas tree will probably be rife with freeloading bugs, sap, and spiderwebs, so give it a good shake before you pack it in the car to keep your living room free of these natural nuisances. Some tree farms even have mechanical shakers that will get the job done, for a fee.

In a recent development, since the primary purpose of buying a power strip is to have additional outlets, we noted how easy (or difficult) it was to use all of the outlets on the strip at the same time. Our goal wasn’t to see how much power we could pull—that depends solely on the circuit—but to see how well the strips were designed for real-world use.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a strip performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we averaged the points to find our top pick and categorize the others by their best use.

Before choosing the best power strip for your needs, consider how and where you plan to use it, as well as the vital factors below.

The right power strip for your needs depends heavily on how it will be used and which devices or equipment will be plugged into it.

The number of outlets you need in a power strip depends on both how many and what type of devices you want to plug into it. Remember that you should not plug high-power-capacity devices into power strips, regardless of the number of outlets. The circuit still limits the power strip.

Industry observers note that power strips can have as few as two outlets or more than 20. These outlets can be standard power outlets, USB-A or USB-C outlets, wide-spaced outlets intended for larger adapters, and specialty connections like ethernet or coaxial connections. The number and configuration of outlets are mostly a personal preference; however, consider that as the number of outlets increases, so does the size of the power strip. So, if space is an matter, choose a power strip with fewer outlets and a narrower profile.

Length and configuration refer to the length of the cord and the type of outlets in the power strip.

Recent findings suggest that in our technologically advanced society, many devices and appliances embedded with complex electrical systems are very sensitive to power surges, so surge protection is a feature of a power strip nearly everyone needs. Power surges typically occur when a storm brings down electrical lines, causing the power manufacturer to reroute power to address power demands. These changes can create inconsistent power flow fluctuations, resulting in a power surge. The only way to protect all appliances and devices is with a whole-house surge protector, but strips with surge protection will reduce the risk of damage to sensitive electronics and devices.

Recent findings suggest that surge protection—also referred to as the surge suppression rating of a power strip—is measured in joules (J) and normally varies, depending on the product, from as low as 100 J to higher than 4,000 J. When using a power strip as surge protection for expensive or sensitive devices, it is important to invest in a power strip with a high surge suppression rating.

A standard power strip runs electricity to multiple devices, typically via an on/off switch. Smart power strips function similarly, but they can also connect with compatible smart home systems, like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, usually through a WiFi connection.

According to recent reports, once a smart power strip connects to a smart home system, consumers can control the electrical supply to the paired devices through either voice control or a smartphone app. Some power strips even support timers or schedules so connected devices will automatically turn on or off.

While power strips don’t seem very dangerous, cords can become trip hazards and electrocution and fires can result from improper use. Many power strip manufacturers include safety features like full-metal housing, internal circuit breakers, or ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) to protect owners and their property from harm.

Take a look below to find the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about electrical power outlet strips.

If used properly, a power strip can actually reduce the risk of electrical fire by providing a safe place to plug in additional accessories. However, if misused, either by overloading it, using it for appliances it’s not rated for, or linking multiple power strips together (called daisy-chaining), a power strip can become a danger.

Never plug high-power-capacity appliances, such as electric space heaters, refrigerators, microwaves, toaster ovens, and air conditioners, into a power strip.

In a recent development, daisy-chaining power strips means linking multiple power strips together in a series that connects back to a single electrical outlet. This is a big concern for fire-fighting professionals because daisy-chained connections will almost invariably lead to an overloaded power strip that heats up until it burns out or catches fire.

Industry observers note that power strips can catch fire if they are old or frayed, or if they are overloaded beyond their capacity. This can happen when several devices that draw too much electricity, such as air conditioners or electric heaters, are plugged into the same strip. The strip will then heat up and eventually begin to melt, sparking a fire.

Recent findings suggest that while there is some discrepancy between specific products, on average, power strips will last for about 2 years before replacement is necessary. However, they can last between 3 to 5 years if properly maintained.

It depends on what you plug into the strips, but in general, it’s not a good practice to plug two strips into one outlet. Overloading the circuit will cause the breaker to trip.

In a home that has too few outlets for the owners’ needs, power strips can absolutely be worth the money because they expand the number of outlets available. Power strips that have surge protection are also ideal for homes with a lot of sensitive electronics, as the strips prevent damage when power surges might otherwise cause damage. Just keep in mind that power strips don’t actually provide more power to the home—they just allow more devices to use the power that’s already there.

It’s not a bad idea. Turning it off will reduce standby energy usage, but as long as you’re not overloading the circuit, it should be safe to leave on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that at the outset of President Trump's second term, there were a number of vacant district court seats throughout Texas.
  • Industry observers note that up to this point, none of the vacancies in the Northern District of Texas were tapped.
  • Industry observers note that but there were still two open seats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at the outset of President Trump's second term, there were a number of vacant district court seats throughout Texas. A reasonable person might have predicted that given two Republican senators, those seats would be filled quickly, but no such luck. The first nomination--Nicholas Ganjei for S.D.Tex--was not made until November 2025. Yes, while Missouri quickly filled all the seats, Texas lagged behind. Two more nominations in the Western District were made in January 2026--Andrew Davis for the Austin seat and Chis Wolfe for the Waco seat. It's worth noting that both Ganjei and Davis served as Chief Counsel for Senator Cruz. And the story of the Waco seat is enough for another post. In April 2026, two more nominations were made for S.D. Tex. seats in the Valley: John Marck and Arthur Jones.

Industry observers note that up to this point, none of the vacancies in the Northern District of Texas were tapped. Finally, in May 2026, Kasdin Mitchell was nominated to one of the seats in N.D. Tex. At that time, Angela Colmenero was tapped for another seat in Houston. Four more months would lapse. In September, Richard Bennett was nominated for a seat in Houston and Courtney Coker was nominated for a seat in Dallas.

Industry observers note that but there were still two open seats. The critical vacancy was the Western District of Texas seat in Austin, which had remained open for some time. Virtually all of the litigation against the state government is filed in Austin. And, for reasons that continue to elude me, David Ezra, a senior judge from Hawaii, brings the Aloha Spirit to muck up Texas jurisprudence.

Shortly after the midterm election, President Trump nominated Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the Austin seat. Around the same time, Trump nominated Elliot Gaiser for the remaining N.D. Tex. in Dallas. Ultimately, Senator Cornyn would block Gaiser's nomination, and urged the White House to nominate Steve Fahey. That's where thing stand now.

Sources indicate that many people, even those in Texas, cannot make sense of this situation. Why on earth did it take so long to fill all of these seats? Why did nominations for the final two seats only come after the election? Why did Trump pick Gaiser if Cornyn had objections?

Let me try to set the record straight on a few matters here.

In a recent development, traditionally, Texas District court nominees have gone through something called the Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee (FJEC). Senators Cornyn and Cruz have used this structure to allow local attorneys (now about 30) to make recommendations on potential judicial candidates. The committee will screen applications, conduct interview, and recommend finalists to the Senators. Generally, if both senators sign off on a finalist, they recommend the name to the White House. At that point, the White House will conduct an interview, and if things work out, a nomination is made. I hedge slightly, because sometimes the process goes in a different order. It can happen that the White House really likes a particular candidate, and speaks to them in parallel, or even before the FJEC process goes through. But FJEC remains a central cog in any district court nomination.

For more than a year, there has been something of a standoff concerning the N.D. Tex. seat. There were two relevant finalists from FJEC. The first was Michael Berry, a Marine Veteran, longtime attorney with the First Liberty Institute, and--perhaps most importantly--former Chief Counsel to Senator Cruz. The second was Steve Fahey, a lawyer I did not know. He was an assistant United States Attorney until 2021, and now has a solo private practice. I'm told one of his most significant case was seeking a writ of coram nobis to protect an illegal alien from deportation. (The petition was denied.).

Senator Cornyn blocked Berry. Or to be more precise, Cornyn's Chief Counsel, Franci Becker, blocked Berry. The exact reason is not entirely clear. I've heard some rumors that Becker blames Berry for blocking another district court nominee, but that never happened. Senator Cruz supported that nominee. The White House found problems in that nom's record that would have made confirmation impossible. Ultimately, she withdrew from the search, and took a lucrative in-house position. Another explanation is that Becker, and Cornyn, opposed Berry because he was too conservative. Whatever the reasons, Berry had deep ties to Texas. The White House had interviewed Berry, and was prepared to make the nomination, but Cornyn kept saying no. The Washington Examiner reports on this story.

What about Fahey? I'm told that Cruz never actually blocked Fahey, but the White House had reservations about the nominee--especially his work defending illegal aliens. Ultimately, the decision was made to just let the seat stay open and it would be filled once Cornyn is out of office. The Austin seat was vital, as it involves so much state-wide litigation, but the Dallas division seats are interchangeable. This is not Amarillo or Wichita Falls. Indeed, even if Paxton were to lose the election, the Senate was likely to stay in Republican control, and a deal could be made with Senator Talarico for the Dallas seat. Alas, the election day bloodbath changed things.

Industry observers note that the Sullivan nomination for the Austin seat was made quite swiftly, even though it had been in the works for a while. Sullivan had already gone through the background check, as well as the FJEC approval. But what about Elliot Gaiser? It is true that Gaiser did not go through FJEC, but he had something very important: a recent FBI background check and Senate confirmation. He could (in theory) be slotted into the final confirmation hearing planned for November 18.

Sources indicate that despite my best efforts, Senator Cornyn blocked Gaiser's nomination. Cornyn (or at least someone on his staff) put out this social media post to explain his actions:.

It has been revealed that if President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience, and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide "advise and consent," which is impossible without consultation.

Sources indicate that still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel. All that is needed is an FBI background check with they stand ready to do on a timely basis.

Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence.

According to recent reports, this post is misleading. Why did Trump wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The short answer is that Cornyn blocked the White House's and Cruz's preferred candidate, and the White House did not want to pick Cornyn's candidate. That's how things work. Senators can withhold consent by not returning a blue slip. But they can't force the White House to make a nomination they don't wish to make. The White House then tried a list-ditch effort to get someone into the seat before the upcoming Congress concluded. I'm sure the administration was hoping that Senator Cornyn would realize that a filled seat is better than an empty seat, but he refused, and blocked Gaiser. Moreover, Cornyn refused to even meet with Gaiser, so he is no position to complain about a "lack of consultation." FJEC could have performed a review of Gaiser on short notice, but it was never convened.

According to recent reports, cornyn states Fahey was "was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee." But that does not mean Senator Cruz himself approved of Fahey. Indeed, Senator Cruz can still withhold a blue slip of Fahey. That comeuppance would be just, after Cornyn blocked both Berry and Gaiser unreasonably. Cornyn has earned no favors at this point--especially after cursing at Cruz on the Senate floor and calling him a "fragile thing" on social media. After the events of the past few weeks, I think James Talarico would be a more trustworthy partner on nominees than Cornyn. Remember, Cornyn aided and abetted the spiking of Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the Eighth Circuit. Soon enough, Judge Ada Brown's NDTX seat will become open--either through resignation or impeachment. I can see a deal being made with Cruz gets one of the Dallas seats and Talarico gets the other. All Cornyn could do that point is grouse.

Sources indicate that the bigger problem is that there is no time left for a hearing. The November 18 hearing was the end of the show. Cornyn's stunt is now putting pressure on Senator Grassley to break even more China by holding a December nomination hearing. There is no reason that Grassley should give Cornyn this courtesy--especially after the recent stunts Cornyn has pulled.

Industry observers note that this post is based on my best understanding of some complex deliberations over the course of nearly two years. If you spot any errors, please send me an email.

Update: Tuesday evening, the press secretary from Senator Cornyn's post reached out and said "It's inaccurate to say that Franci Becker is responsible for blocking Mike Berry's nomination." She asked me to post a statement, which I will do:.

Attributable to a Cornyn spokesperson, Franci Becker did not block Mike Berry's nomination, as staff in Senate offices do not have the authority to make decisions about a nominee, and the claims in this story were not corroborated by Sen. Cornyn's office.

Of course, the ultimate decision to sign a blue slip belongs to the Senator. In any office, a staffer cannot take a final action. So in a hyper-technical sense, no staffer is capable of blocking any nominee. But Chief Counsels routinely make decisions about candidates that their senators defer to.

Industry observers note that what the statement does not say is far more important than what it actually notes. There is no denial along the lines of, "Franci Becker played no role in Mike Berry not receiving a blue slip." I also posed a few other questions about Becker's involvement with the Dallas seat, that the press secretary did not answer.

Sources indicate that I stand by what I wrote, which is something I have heard from multiple sources in the Senate over the course of nearly a year. Staffers from other Senator's offices thanked me for this post. Two federal judges who are familiar with the situation thanked me for writing this. People I trust and who are familiar with the situation reviewed it and found no errors.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

The holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

In a recent development, A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

Learn what a roofing expert says about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

A post shared by Drew (@thedrewsocial).

Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing tech giant in Illinois.

“That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski says. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create challenges with moisture.”.

The cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

According to recent reports, chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

Rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski claims.

Sources indicate that wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

According to recent reports, moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”.

A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

Homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

Roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

For homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

California ordered Waymo off freeways after troubling encounters with road crews and police. Here's what happened and how riders are affected.

Driving through a construction zone can be confusing, especially when lanes are closed or police are directing traffic. Waymo’s self-driving cars have run into problems in these situations, too.

On Nov. 11, California banned Waymo from operating driverless vehicles on freeways following several incidents involving road crews and police. The firm has since stopped freeway rides in other states as well.

Here’s why California stepped in and what the ban means for Waymo passengers.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) noted the incidents put construction workers and other drivers at risk.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near Burlingame, where crews were working. Waymo noted no one was injured, and no collisions occurred.

The next day, another Waymo attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles during a traffic break on Interstate 280. Officers use traffic breaks to slow or stop vehicles, often because of roadwork or a hazard ahead. Drivers must stay behind the patrol cars until officers allow traffic to resume.

Industry observers note that waymo had similar problems in May, which led to a temporary suspension and software changes. But new incidents occurred in November.

According to recent reports, in April, California approved stricter rules for self-driving cars. DMV Director Steve Gordon mentioned the changes would bring “additional accountability for AV manufacturers.”.

According to recent reports, the freeway ban doesn’t affect Waymo’s regular street service, although some trips may take longer. Waymo has also voluntarily stopped commercial freeway rides in other states while it looks into what went wrong.

Waymo’s cars use cameras and sensors to monitor traffic, but construction zones don’t always follow normal traffic patterns. The recent incidents highlighted problems with how the vehicles responded to road closures and police activity.

There’s no date yet for Waymo to return to California freeways. The DMV wants the manufacturer to show that its cars can safely handle road closures and police activity before allowing driverless freeway rides again.

Industry observers note that waymo says it’s working with state officials and will continue testing on freeways with trained specialists behind the wheel. Passengers can still book rides on regular streets in the meantime.

#148569. Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)

Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here's what real-world crash data actually says about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.
  • Recent findings suggest that giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes.
  • Industry observers note that yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Here's what real-world crash data actually says about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.

Recent findings suggest that giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes. A logging truck traveling down a busy highway spills its cargo and sets off a chain reaction of intense car crashes. It’s a gruesome, cinematic disaster, but the basic danger is grounded in reality. Logs can come loose during transport, with serious consequences on a busy road. Has anything like the Final Destination truck scene actually happened in real life?

Industry observers note that yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents. However, the Final Destination truck scene depicting this realistic road hazard is grossly exaggerated. Logs can fall off of trucks and cause accidents, but they don’t bounce down the highway and become windshield-level projectiles like in the film. So, yes, the danger is real, but the chain-reaction chaos depicted in the film is highly dramatized.

In January 2024, a logging truck on Interstate 95 in Florida overturned while traveling too fast through a curve in the road. Logs spilled onto the highway, rolled over a barrier and into oncoming traffic. A Jacksonville man who was involved in the accident told local reporters, “I just had a real life Final Destination moment…” However, he and all other motorists were unharmed. In June of 2025, another turnover dumped not logs, but large metal pipes across Highway 75 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, closing both lanes of traffic. Again, no injuries were reported. A fatal accident involving a logging truck did occur in Arkansas in 2014. While traveling down Highway 65, the truck blew a rear tire, swerved into a bridge construction site and tipped over. Two construction workers were killed by the discharged logs.

Each year, shifting or unsecured loads carried by commercial vehicles are linked to roughly 4,000 to 7,000 accidents. This may not sound like a lot, but these accidents have severe consequences, often resulting in serious injury or death. “They regularly make news headlines, so the average person may think they’re more common than they are,” personal injury attorney Juan Dominguez indicates. In fact, the most dangerous vehicles carrying cargo are non-commercial cars and trucks. 73 percent of highway accidents involving road debris are caused by passenger vehicles with unsecured loads. Commercial trucks are closely regulated and inspected for proper load security, contributing to lower accident rates. Despite the attention given to logging truck accidents, they are only involved in 1.5 percent of all fatal commercial truck accidents each year.

Take control of your safety when sharing the road with large cargo trucks. Here’s how:.

Industry observers note that “My first rule is to never drive directly behind a truck with a [loose] load like logs, pipes or steel beams,” construction safety specialist Steven Menotti indicates. “If the load shifts or falls off, you’ll be the first vehicle it hits.” If you have to drive behind a cargo truck,  increase your following distance to at least four seconds, which allows for more reaction time if debris falls into the road. “That distance can help if the unexpected happens and something comes loose,” Dominguez says. “You have more time to try and react.” If possible, reduce your speed for a shorter stopping distance.

It has been revealed that if you need to pass a truck on the highway, time it so you can quickly complete the pass and return to the lane. Avoid driving directly next to a cargo truck for an extended length of time to avoid being hit by falling debris or cargo.

According to recent reports, if you spot a truck without a properly secured load, move away from it on the road. Look for worn or loose straps and chains, unevenly loaded cargo or missing side stakes. “Those all indicate the trucker probably didn’t check the load,” Menotti claims. “I won’t follow it. I change lanes, and pull far back.”.

Sources indicate that logs can fall from trucks, but they don’t bounce or become projectiles across the highway like the Final Destination truck scene. In the film, this depiction was CGI-generated.

Sources indicate that brake hard and avoid swerving. Swerving causes 37 percent of all road debris accident fatalities, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Clear the counter clutter and fuel your mornings with a scrap-wood coffee station that has a spot for everything.

According to recent reports, if you know three things about me, it’s that I’m a stickler for organization, I run on coffee, and I can’t throw away wood scraps. This coffee station checks all three boxes.

Industry observers note that it’s built almost entirely from maple offcuts, which explains the mix of thicknesses on the Cutting List. To keep it approachable, every joint is a simple butt joint with glue and brad nails. Biscuits are used only for the glued-up panels. If you can make square cuts and run a nailer, you can build this in a weekend.

[Please insert TA “Coffee_org_case.pdf” here with callouts.].

[Please insert TA “Coffee_org_drawer.pdf” here with callouts.].

Boards wide enough for the top (A) and base (B) are almost impossible to find, so I made the panels by joining several boards with biscuits.

According to recent reports, cut the boards at least 1/2-in. longer and wider than needed. The extra material lets you trim the panels square and to size after the glue dries.

It has been revealed that mark across each joint where you want a biscuit, spacing them 6- to 8-in. apart and about 3-in. from each end. Cut the slots with a biscuit joiner. Be generous with the glue in the slots and along the edges. You want an even bead of squeeze-out so you know you have good coverage. Clamp the panels and keep them flat as they dry.

Recent findings suggest that once the glue dries, scrape off the squeeze-out and cut the top (A) and base (B) to the final size. Then cut the rest of the parts following the cutting list.

Connect the two sides (C) and the back (E) to the base (B) of the coffee organizer using 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Secure the sides so they’re flush with the bottom of the base. Set the back on the base between the sides, flush with the back edges of the base (B) and sides (C).

Cut the pieces for the butcher block (L) and biscuit-join them the same way you did the panels. Again, cut them at least 1/2-in. oversize. That allows for the wood shifting during clamping and leaves enough on each end to make clean, square cuts once the glue has dried.

It has been revealed that once the glue is dry, cut the butcher block to final size on the table saw. Scrape and sand off the dried glue, then round over the sharp edges with a router and a bearing-guided 1/4-in. round-over bit.

Recent findings suggest that when you size the butcher block, leave room for the drawer slides you’ll install later. Most need about 1/2-in. on each side, so a 13-in. opening takes a 12-in.-wide butcher block.

Industry observers note that the left-hand compartment houses the butcher block and drawer, so it needs to be 13-in. wide: 12-in. for the butcher block and drawer, plus 1-in. for the drawer slides. Mark the divider location, then test-fit the butcher block and loose drawer slides to confirm the opening. Apply glue and secure the center divider (D) with 18-gauge brad nails driven up through the base (B) and in through the back (E).

In a recent development, note: Drawer slide clearance varies by style and manufacturer. Check your slides’ specs and adjust the opening as needed.

Industry observers note that build a drawer to store coffee pods and spoons. Glue and nail the drawer box front and back (G) to the ends of the sides (F), then attach the bottom (H) to square it up. The drawer front (K) covers the nails on the front.

Industry observers note that secure the drawer dividers (J) inside the drawer (Fig. B) with wood glue and brad nails, spacing them to fit your coffee pods, spoons, or other items. Feel free to add or take away dividers as needed. I left 1-1/2-in.-wide slots for pods and a 4-in.-wide slot for spoons.

Industry observers note that on the left side of the coffee organizer, install the butcher block (L) and drawer using your drawer slides and the included hardware. Both attach to the left side (C) and center divider (D), so install the butcher block first and the drawer above it. Pre-drill and hand-screw for proper alignment and to avoid stripping the screws.

It has been revealed that once the butcher block (L) and drawer are installed, cover the left compartment with the top (A), securing it with glue and 18-gauge brad nails. The right side stays open.

It has been revealed that then attach the drawer front (K) to the drawer box front so it overlaps the left side (C) and center divider (D). Use double-sided tape to position it and 1-in. screws from inside the drawer box to lock it down.

Install and secure dividers on the right side of the unit with 1-1/4-inch 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Working from the front to the back of the coffee station:.

In the 6-1/4-in. space between the front face (M) and the short divider (N), install the tea separators (R) and spacers (S and T) to make a divided area for sugar, teas, stirrers, etc. Use a 23-gauge nailer and 5/8-in. nails to secure the spacers (S and T) to the front face (M) and short divider (N), then slide the tea separators (R) into the gaps between them. My compartments were 2-1/8-in. and 3-in. wide, but feel free to make them whatever size you’d like.

Recent findings suggest that sink any protruding nails, fill the nail holes with wood filler, and finish-sand the entire piece. Apply a finish to the whole unit. I used Tried & True Original Wood Finish, which is food-safe, so it works on the butcher block and everything else.

According to recent reports, then install the handles on the drawer and butcher block. You can’t reach behind the solid butcher block to drive a screw, so cut the head off the handle screw with a hacksaw, drill a pilot hole, and glue the cut end into it with CA glue or epoxy.

In a recent development, A food-safe wood finish won’t transfer chemicals or toxins to the food when being used. There are two ways a finish is considered food-safe. Either it is completely non-toxic and edible in its liquid state from its origin, or, once fully cured, the VOCs (volatile organic compounds) in the finish disperse, and it becomes a stable, inert, non-toxic solid. Finishes like food-grade mineral oil or fractionated coconut oil are considered food-safe from the time of application and work well as food-safe wood finishes.

A coffee station should include options for coffee or tea, sweeteners, flavoring and stirring. Focus on organization and easy access tiers – no matter what you choose to present in your coffee station.

Recent findings suggest that 42-in. works well for a free-standing coffee station cabinet. This is slightly higher than a standard 36-in. countertop height and lower than a 45-in. bar height top. For a coffee station on a countertop beneath upper cabinets, you want enough clearance to open and close your coffee maker’s lid. A 6-in. tall coffee station would give you 12-in. clearance in a standard 18-in. opening between the top of the counter and the bottom of the upper cabinets.

Latest Update: No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D.
  • [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so.
  • In a recent development, in Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Staton v. Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D. Pa.) Oct. 15, but just noted a few days ago in the Westlaw Bulletin:.

[Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so. She relies on a document entitled "Patient Specimen Release Form" which she signed on August 22, 2021. In her prayer for relief, plaintiff seeks the award of "compensatory and consequential damages against [Jefferson] … in an amount to be determined at trial, based on the unique personal, cultural and spiritual value of Ms. Staton's placenta." In addition, she asks the court to "[g]rant such other and further relief as the Court deems just, equitable, and proper." ….

In a recent development, in Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract. The parties have cited no case and this court has found none where the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania has ever held that emotional distress damages are recoverable in a breach of contract action. However, in D'Ambrosio, v. Pennsylvania National Mutual Casualty Insurance Co. (1981) the Court left the door open….:.

The possibility cannot be ruled out that emotional distress damages may be recoverable on a contract where, for example, "the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result." ….

[Restatement (Second) of Contracts §] 353, which the Pennsylvania Supreme Court referenced by a different number in D'Ambrosio, precludes emotional damages except in very limited circumstances:.

Recovery for emotional disturbance will be excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or the contract or the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result.

The Restatement gives examples in Comment a. of cases which fit into the second exception. They are contracts for the proper disposition of a dead body, contracts for the carriage of messages concerning death, and contracts of carriers and innkeepers with passengers and guests….

Recent findings suggest that in this court's view, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would follow the general rule that emotional damages are not recoverable in contract cases…. While contracts for the proper disposition of dead bodies allow for distress damages under § 353, plaintiff concedes that she "does not equate a placenta with a decedent's remains.".

In opposing to the pending motion, plaintiff stresses her allegations that her placenta had personal, cultural, and spiritual value to her and that she suffered emotional distress when it was not returned to her. Even if true, her subjective reaction to the alleged breach of contract is not relevant to the glitch before the court. In Pennsylvania, emotional distress damages are generally not recoverable in a breach of contract action. Whether emotional distress damages would ever be recoverable would depend on the type of contract or breach alleged, not on the plaintiff's emotional or mental state.

According to recent reports, the standard set forth in § 353 is an objective one. No case suggests that the application of § 353 or the allowance of emotional distress damages would be decided based on the effect of the breach on the particular plaintiff without regard to the type of contract or breach involved. Otherwise, the floodgates would be open to emotional distress damages in virtually every breach of contract action….

The result might in principle have been different in a tort lawsuit for conversion, since emotional distress damages are generally available in such torts; but it's not clear that ejected parts of the body such as the placenta would be treated as property under Pennsylvania law for conversion purposes.

Joseph Hoynoski and Jeffrey Chomco (Marshall Dennehey, P.C.) represent defendants.
