    #148525. The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2719 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    Industry observers note that satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each newly introduced matter at the outset?

    Sources indicate that chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of fresh datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material issues in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or matter. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    Sources indicate that satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every new tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    It has been revealed that ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    Sources indicate that satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same strategy from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    Industry observers note that satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client says it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati remarked earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Industry observers note that satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    Chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely important, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be noted in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    Chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    US Tries but Fails to Dilute UN Human Rights Resolutions

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
    • The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.
    • Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

    The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.

    Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.

    At the Third Committee, the US targeted language in draft resolutions referencing sexual and reproductive rights for women and girls. For resolutions on violence against women and girls and trafficking in women and girls, the US proposed adding “in accordance with national laws” after such references. The proposed amendments reflect the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle internationally protected reproductive rights.

    Industry observers note that the US has not been acting alone. Russia proposed deleting an ICC reference from the resolution on trafficking in women and girls. Egypt submitted similar amendments to the resolution on violence against women and girls and sought to remove a reference to “sexual orientation and gender identity” from a resolution on extrajudicial executions.

    UN member countries rejected the amendments and adopted the resolutions.

    According to recent reports, the US also voted against a resolution supporting human rights defenders because it included references to gender and reproductive rights. It abstained on human rights resolutions it traditionally supports on North Korea, Myanmar, and Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia because of ICC references. Those resolutions also passed.

    It has been revealed that the Trump administration’s assault on the international human rights system has not been limited to UN resolutions. It has imposed sanctions on ICC judges, prosecutors, nongovernmental groups, a UN human rights expert, and the court itself. It has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick” to prevent investigations of US and Israeli officials.

    It has been revealed that it’s heartening that these attempts by the US and others to undermine human rights and international accountability have failed so far. But UN member countries need to work together to resist future efforts to weaken human rights norms and international justice.

    Tech Report: Fifth Circuit Dismisses Lawsuit Over Facebook Removal, Supposedly Connected to Stanford Internet Observatory, of COVID-Related Post

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that from Hines v.
    • Jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19.
    • This case is closely related to Murthy v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that from Hines v. Stamos, decided yesterday by Judges W. Eugene Davis, Leslie Southwick, and Stuart Kyle Duncan:.

    Jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19. The district court dismissed her suit without prejudice for lack of subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Because Hines has not shown that her injury is fairly traceable to Stanford or Stamos, she lacks standing. We therefore AFFIRM without reaching personal jurisdiction….

    This case is closely related to Murthy v. Missouri, which guides our resolution of this appeal. In Murthy, Hines (along with others) sued federal officials and agencies, alleging the government censored her online speech against COVID-19 restrictions in violation of the First Amendment. Here, Hines challenges Defendants' participation in an academic project named the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP). She alleges the EIP and its participants aided the government's scheme to have Facebook suppress her online speech, also in violation of the First Amendment. {Our review is limited to Hines's claims against Stanford and Alex Stamos, the former director of the Stanford Internet Observatory, which was an EIP member.}.

    In a recent development, facebook began moderating COVID-19 content early in the pandemic, deleting or demoting posts it deemed false. In April 2020 alone, it labeled roughly 50 million pieces of content. That same month, Hines launched a grassroots campaign to challenge COVID-19 government restrictions and used Facebook to communicate with her supporters. She was aware of Facebook's moderation and took deliberate measures to circumvent it.

    The EIP, a consortium of researchers and institutions, was formed in July 2020. It sought to identify misinformation about elections and voting. For about three months in 2020, it monitored elections-related content on social media. EIP participants sometimes recommended actions to social-media platforms and logged their communications when they did. In most instances, the platforms took no detectable action on those recommendations….

    To have standing, a "plaintiff must have (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision." For the claims before us, the second inquiry—traceability of Hines's past injuries—is "the whole ball game." ….

    Industry observers note that there is one injury that Hines claims is traceable to Defendants: on September 9, 2020, Facebook removed a post from Hines's page that attached an article entitled Masks Don't Work. At the time, Facebook explained the post went "against our Community Standards." It also reduced distribution of Hines's page on COVID-19 restrictions for "repeated" violations of its standards on "Inauthentic Behavior" and for "repeated sharing of false news." Hines does not dispute that these restrictions fit Facebook's own content moderation….

    Hines's traceability theory rests on an inference drawn from timing. On September 8, 2020, the EIP received a massive submission of over 200 webpages and social-media posts from the Democratic National Committee. Among those 200 webpages was a single post by Hines where she encouraged her followers to lobby their representatives to end the COVID-19 public-health emergency. In Hines's view, the one-day timing between the DNC's submission and Facebook's moderation of her page is evidence that EIP participants called Facebook's attention to her single post in the 200-webpage DNC submission.

    According to recent reports, we are not persuaded by her argument. Discovery revealed no communication between the EIP and Facebook about Hines, and Facebook did not remove or moderate the post that the EIP received. {Hines argues there may be evidence of Defendants' communications with Facebook in undiscovered Slack or Zoom messages. But Stanford produced "communications and other documents" mentioning Hines or her account, and Hines neither challenged that production nor moved to compel additional discovery, although the scheduling order allowed for that. The mere possibility of undiscovered communications that were not sought in the district court is not evidence.}.

    Industry observers note that A notation in the EIP's records even says Hines's COVID-19 posts were beyond the scope of the EIP's elections-oriented work. We conclude as a matter of law that timing alone is too attenuated to trace Hines's injury to Defendants.

    Industry observers note that murthy also requires us to consider Facebook's own incentives to moderate content. Facebook gave its own reasons for acting when it removed Hines's post and demoted her page, and Hines does not dispute that that moderation aligned with Facebook's COVID-19 policies. We agree with the district court that there's no indication that Facebook, in moderating Hines's post, did anything other than follow its own moderation policy….

    I am not at all involved with Stanford's defense of this lawsuit.

    According to recent reports, elisabeth S. Theodore, John B. Bellinger, III, R. Stanton Jones, and Stephen K. Wirth (Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer, L.L.P.) and James A. Brown (Liskow & Lewis, A.P.L.C.) represent defendants.

    • Recent findings suggest that (Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on issues including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026.

    Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on issues including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

    It has been revealed that “Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” noted Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.”.

    According to recent reports, vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression, reaching beyond the country’s borders to suppress dissent by targeting human rights activists, government critics, and others in violation of their human rights. In late September, the overseas political organization Viet Tan alleged that Vietnamese police had detained three of its members in Cambodia, including Tran Hiep, and transferred them to Vietnam.

    The Vietnamese government at the moment holds more than 160 political prisoners for exercising their rights to free expression or for peacefully advocating human rights and democracy. Dozens more are detained and awaiting trial. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists to lengthy prison terms, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan. During this period, the police arrested at least 46 other people for criticizing the government.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming dialogue should also focus on Vietnam’s suppression of independent labor organizing. Both Australia and Vietnam are parties to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, which contains provisions obligating Vietnam to carry out reforms and to allow the creation of independent trade unions. However, as Human Rights Watch recently documented, the Vietnamese government has not actually reformed its policies and practices, and prevents workers from forming and operating genuinely independent unions.

    The Australian government should communicate concerns about these violations. It should also outline how Vietnam’s failures to reform will affect Australia-Vietnam relations and implementation of trade and tariff provisions in the partnership.

    Sources indicate that “The Australia-Vietnam human rights dialogue will accomplish little so long as concrete outcomes aren’t formalized,” Gavshon stated. “A human rights dialogue shouldn’t be a box-ticking exercise but instead a diplomatic exchange with real-world implications.”.

    Newly introduced in Civitas Outlook: "Justice Kagan Cries Wolf"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • My latest essay in Civitas Outlook combines much of my recent thinking about Justice Kagan.
    • Here is the introduction of Justice Kagan Cries Wolf:.
    • Justice Elena Kagan recently confessed, "I'm much better in print than I am in person." She's right.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    My latest essay in Civitas Outlook combines much of my recent thinking about Justice Kagan. She has shifted to different modalities of persuasion over her career on the bench. The latest front is to preemptively blame the Court for destroying democracy and then complain how the Court's legitimacy is being wounded. She is like the arsonist who seeks mercy for burning down her own house. The bigger problem is her predictions are simply wrong. Kagan has some serious crow to eat after the blue tsunami. An entire jurisprudence based on consequentialism fails if the consequences never happen.

    Here is the introduction of Justice Kagan Cries Wolf:.

    Justice Elena Kagan recently confessed, "I'm much better in print than I am in person." She's right. Through a series of carefully coordinated public appearances, Justice Kagan has attempted to influence how her colleagues vote and how the public perceives the Court. Worse still, Kagan made dire predictions about how the Court has wounded democracy and its own legitimacy. But in short order, the midterm elections refuted her consequentialism. Elena Kagan is the Justice who cries wolf. Justices should speak through their judicial writings, not try to distort the process from the sidelines. . . .

    This sort of consequentialist judging carries a distinct risk: what if the consequences never manifest? In other words, a jurisprudence based on predicting certain outcomes fails if the predictions are wrong. Kagan did not just try to predict the outcome of the midterm election; she proclaimed she could divine the future of our republic. Alas, in short order, Justice Kagan has proven herself to be less Cook Report and more Miss Cleo.

    Recent findings suggest that kagan's point seems to be that ruling against the President who appoints you is proof you're a fair justice. That premise holds only if the law does not support the appointing President's policy. If a Justice simply rules against the President who appoints him, then the Justice is no longer a judge. In his upcoming book So Ordered, Justice Alito chides so-called "insecure originalists" who favor outcomes that yield results they dislike to bolster a reputation of independence. Alito, "Twenty-first-century originalists should shed this insecure mindset." Yet Kagan intentionally feeds into this insecurity.

    Justice Kagan, and all Justices, cannot predict the consequences of their decisions. Chief Justice Roberts can predict a decade-long "long game" no better than Kagan can predict the outcome of a single midterm election. They should stop trying to see into the future. Accordingly, the Justices should not be cowed into altering their rulings based on doomsday predictions of what might happen. As for Justice Kagan, the parable of the girl who cries wolf is on point. She can keep speaking, but we don't have to listen.

    My point here echoes my point about the Chief Justice last summer. The conservatives should stop listening to colleagues who do not put the Constitution's best interest at heart.

    November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both remarked they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that fresh candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that newly introduced candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

    “Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

    “A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

    Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

    “The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith mentioned to Law.com.

    Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

    According to recent reports, “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith remarked. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s important to look at their options early.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Australia revealed on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Although these sanctions are a welcome step, they are long overdue and don’t go far enough.

    It has been revealed that the situation in the West Bank is dire. State-backed settler violence has risen to all-time highs. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced and 1,394 killed by settlers or soldiers in the West Bank since the start of 2023. The number of illegal Israeli settlements has nearly doubled, including the E1 settlement project, which even Israel’s allies have called a “red line,” and which Israeli ministers openly boast is intended to erase any possibility of a future Palestinian state.

    Sources indicate that on the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom announced sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government. The individuals and companies sanctioned by Australia, however, have previously been sanctioned by the United Kingdom and other states.

    When the United Kingdom, France, and Canada revealed a ban on Israel’s illegal settlements in September, Australia did not join. Instead, at the time, Foreign Minister Wong promised further sanctions to deter illegal settlement, which are the ones just announced.

    Israel’s settlements are illegal. In its 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that all states have an obligation to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” Banning trade with illegal settlements isn’t optional. It’s required by international law.

    Industry observers note that australia notes it is genuinely committed to upholding international law while continuing to trade with unlawful settlements that rob Palestinians of their land and livelihoods. Recent reporting suggested that the majority of agricultural shipments coming to Australia marked as “products of Israel” are from illegal settlements.

    It’s past time for Australia to do everything in its power to stop the expansion of settlements, both through a trade ban and targeted sanctions on construction companies engaged in illegal settlement expansion.

    Tech Report: Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bob Woodward's new book is a bit unusual.
    • Sources indicate that beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak.
    • According to recent reports, scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bob Woodward's new book is a bit unusual. There is no coherent narrative or flow. Each chapter simply tells the story of another one of his sources. Chapters 36 through 43 walk through his interviews with Supreme Court Justices, law clerks, and others for The Brethren. The book is a collection of his recollections, mostly from recorded memos, and what all of his source said.

    Sources indicate that beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak. He invariably starts by finding someone low on the totem pole, building trust, and working his way up.

    According to recent reports, scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country. The names of all the law clerks, past and present, was readily available public information. I cannot underscore enough how crucial it is in journalism to focus on the low end of the totem pole. Presidents, justices, cabinet officials are all important interviews.

    In a recent development, what began as a somewhat random "catch-as-catch-can" for Scott and me helped us get inside, as we used what we collected to dig deeper. Quoting information or documents we already possessed helped give confidence to other clerks who would then sometimes reach into their own archives to add details and documents. . . .

    According to recent reports, most of the information in our book, The Brethren, is based on interviews with more than 200 people, including five justices who talked, 170 former and current law clerks, and several dozen former employees of the court. Virtually all the interviews were conducted on deep background, meaning that the identity of the sources would be kept confidential for their lifetimes but all the information could be used in the book. Since all of the justices are now deceased, I am lifting the lid on our interviews with them.

    This sort of journalism takes time and time and more time. But eventually, he has enough information that principals feel comfortable talking to him. And even if he learned what happened from multiple sources, asking yet another source opens up the possibility for even more insights to be gleaned.

    Industry observers note that chapter 36 recounts Woodward's interactions with Justice Stewart, who invited the reporter to his home for an interview. Stewart spoke very critically of Chief Justice Burger. That interview convinced Woodward there was enough to write a book. The publisher gave him and Scott Armstrong a $300,000 advance. That is more than $1.5 million in present-day value.

    Chapter 37 recounts Woodward's interview with Justice Powell. Powell invited him to the Court—right away. Woodward arrived at 4:30 p.m. that day. Powell remarked, "Intellectually there is no Brandeis or Frankfurter or Cardozo on the court now." I've made similar comments since Justice Scalia's passing. I wonder if any members of the current Court think they are at the intellectual level of Holmes or Story? I appreciate Powell's humility.

    Recent findings suggest that woodward would interview Powell two more times. I found these comments about Roe striking:.

    Recent findings suggest that I asked him about the Supreme Court's landmark 1973 abortion decisions in Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton, which legalized abortion nationwide. "It was hard for me and I was frankly strongly result oriented," Powell mentioned of the decision. "I would support abortion funding by the states if I was in the legislature," he added. This caught me off-guard and seemed contrary to the opinions he had written saying there was no right to a state-funded abortion.

    It has been revealed that "I thought the abortion laws were atrocious," Powell continued, referring to the state abortion laws prohibiting abortion. "If you wanted to pay for an abortion you could get one." I noted his selection of the word "wanted" instead of "could afford" which was a significant part of the glitch as I saw it.

    Recent findings suggest that there should be no doubt that Roe was an outcome-driven decision. There was no law—just policy.

    Chapter 38 focuses on how he interviewed more than 170 law clerks. Powell authorized his law clerks to speak to Woodward. Burger's former clerks were "at times the most helpful," especially since Woodward never bothered asking Burger to speak. I already recounted the story in which he "borrowed" Justice Brennan's history of the Watergate tape case.

    Chapter 39 explains how Justice Powell thought the Justices should talk to reporters to minimize the bad press. Powell wrote in a draft letter to Burger that he never sent: "I had rather someone on the Court discussed this with him accurately than leave him to reach his own conclusions with the right to say that he was stonewalled by the Justices.".

    Chapter 40 discusses Armstrong's interview with Justice Blackmun, and the resulting "19-page single-spaced memo." There were a few useful nuggets. Blackmun appreciated how he wasn't Nixon's first or even second choice for the seat.

    "I am humbled by the fact that I was number three, not the number one choice," Blackmun said of his appointment to the Supreme Court. Nixon's first choice, Clement Haynsworth, a federal judge from South Carolina, and second choice, G. Harrold Carswell, a federal judge from Florida, were rejected narrowly in brutal public fights, largely over concerns that Nixon was attempting to shift the court's ideology, which of course he was. Blackmun had been confirmed unanimously in May 1970 in a 94-to-0 vote. "A scarecrow could get nominated after what had happened," Blackmun continued. "It was a difficult period for the Senate. A number of [senators] told me that they wanted to get it over with. They had a real sense of relief that an average guy had come along with whom they couldn't find much wrong.".

    I wonder if Justice Kennedy ever had similar marks of humility, as a fellow third-choice?

    Blackmun was also assigned the Roe opinion because Chief didn't want to take the heat:.

    Recent findings suggest that blackmun said he was well aware that no matter what he wrote, the opinion would be controversial and he would be hated and vilified. The chief could not afford to take on such a controversial case himself, particularly from the minority. "That's why I was assigned the abortion memo. We were scattered on it," Blackmun said. Douglas was the court's mischievous liberal, the rebel, and couldn't be the author. Any abortion opinion Douglas wrote would be widely questioned outside the court. Brennan was a firm vote for striking down the state abortion laws, but he was the court's only sitting Catholic. As such, Brennan could not be expected to take the heat from the Catholic anti-abortion groups. Marshall could not author for similar reasons: An opinion by the court's only Black man could be perceived as specifically designed for Black people or incite race-fueled blame for the decision. Stewart would have trouble going very far… That left one option: Blackmun.

    It has been revealed that by Chapter 41, the first draft of the book was complete. Now, Powell declined to talk further with Woodward.

    Chapter 42 recounts a fairly gruff interview with Justice White, who gave up virtually nothing.

    Chapter 43 relays how Justice Powell wrote to Chief Justice Burger about the upcoming book. Powell, of course, did not disclose how he spoke with Woodward, and how he authorized his clerks to do the same. I can get Burger's frustration.

    Chief Justice Warren Burger erupted in a letter back to Powell, squarely blaming the clerks and noting "there are hazards in talking with certain 'categories' in this life"—meaning me and Scott, or reporters in general. He criticized the clerks for seeming to have succumbed to the "glamour" of rubbing shoulders with "print names!" . . .

    I wondered if Burger knew that five of the seven justices in his ranks had talked to us and several had given their clerks permission to assist us.

    If only Burger knew that Powell and others blabbed. I suspect Chief Justice Roberts can relate.

    It also turns out that Woodward asked a young Stephen Breyer to fact-check the book.

    In a recent development, another secret that has a certain historic value today was that one weekend before The Brethren went to the printers, a young man named Stephen Breyer came over to my home. He sat in the living room and read the book cover to cover. At that time he was chief counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee chaired by Senator Ted Kennedy. Scott had insisted we have the book's use of legal terms checked for obvious errors. After reading, Breyer told us it was "a hell of a book.".

    I would note there is no discussion of interviewing Justice Rehnquist, even though Rehnquist is named as a source. Something is off.

    Industry observers note that that's it. Nothing earth-shattering. But it is a shame Woodward decided to relay non-public communications with Breyer and Kagan, who are both alive and well.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

    During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who said these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

    People told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

    Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

    According to media reports, armed groups have also carried out six attacks using drones armed with explosives in Catatumbo in the first half of November, killing at least five people, including one civilian, and injuring 14 civilians.

    The situation in Catatumbo has been critical since early 2025, when Human Rights Watch documented that armed groups killed, assaulted, kidnapped, disappeared civilians and caused the displacement of more than 100,000 people.

    In a recent development, according to official announcements, since President De la Espriella took office in August, the government has carried out three airstrikes in Catatumbo, resulting in 10 deaths. The strikes were followed by Colombian army ground operations that resulted in six arrests, and the recovery of two children who had been recruited by armed groups. Community members told us these actions have done little to reduce armed groups’ violence and control over communities.

    The government should urgently protect civilians, by ensuring that its security strategy goes beyond military operations. It should include effective law enforcement and criminal prosecutions, a stronger humanitarian response, support for affected communities, and targeted social and economic policies to reduce the high levels of poverty that fuel the strength of armed groups in the region.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    According to recent reports, between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006. Israeli soldiers were present in 26.5 percent of such incidents documented by the Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din between September 27 and October 14. The Israeli military has detained hundreds of people trying to protect Palestinian farmers during their harvest, according to local media reports.

    “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” mentioned Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. “Rather than stopping settler violence, the Israeli military is detaining the people trying to ensure that Palestinian farmers can safely harvest their olives.”.

    In a recent development, human Rights Watch interviewed four activists organizing groups or volunteers protecting Palestinians harvesting their olives, two of whom had been detained and released since 2025. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Israeli military on November 16; its responses are reflected below.

    Settler violence in the West Bank has been steadily rising since the current Netanyahu government took office in December 2022. Settlers responsible for attacks operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state. Attacks by armed settlers often occur alongside Israeli army units or with soldiers standing by.

    Absent state protection, Palestinian communities and activists have organized to protect themselves using a tactic called protective presence. This is a form of nonviolent activism and human rights monitoring where international, Israeli, and Palestinian volunteers physically accompany vulnerable communities.

    “[Their presence helps] to deter settlers, or have less violent attacks, and speed up the harvest so people do not have to stay for long exposed in the areas,” Rabie Abu Naim, a Palestinian farmer and activist from Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of Ramallah, told Human Rights Watch.

    However, the international presence is no longer able to deter settler attacks, or the military’s obstruction of the harvest. “I have been doing this for more than ten years,” an organizer stated. “What we used to think could protect farmers no longer works. Since 2023, all red lines have been crossed.”.

    Abu Naim described recent attacks by settlers in Al-Mughayyir, including beatings, burning cars, use of tear gas, and stopping cars on the road: “Anyone who takes the road to Abu-Falah on the western side of the village, which is now the only entry to Al-Mughayyir, states their shahada [the Islamic declaration of faith, noted as final words before dying]. They are entering an ambush … they either survive or they don’t.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “This year’s olive harvest season is one of the worst that Al-Mughayyir ever knew,” Abu Naim stated. “[Settler attacks] are becoming an hourly thing, not daily.”.

    Industry observers note that abu Naim was arrested in October 2025 and administratively detained for nine months. “I suspect it was because of coordinating [protection during] the olive harvest season,” he noted.

    Sources indicate that al-Mughayyir’s farmers have been steadily losing access to their olive groves. In August 2025, the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command signed an order for the uprooting of olive trees on 300 dunams (30 hectares) of land in Al-Mughayyir, ostensibly for security reasons after a Palestinian reportedly shot and wounded a settler who had trespassed on the village’s land. According to Israeli human rights group Kerem Navot, settlers from the Shiloh area carried out clearing operations on about 620 dunams (62 hectares), more than twice the area covered by the order, then took over parts of the land.

    “This year, there are no [protection] campaigns for Al-Mughayyir, because there are no lands we can access,” Abu Naim said. “This year’s season, we can say that there isn’t a harvest.”.

    The Israeli human rights organization Peace Now reported in October that the Israeli military had signed orders barring Palestinians from entering approximately 88,300 dunams (around 21,800 acres) of land in the West Bank, 30 percent more than in 2025, unless they coordinate with the military in advance. The military barred Israeli citizens from only 6,890 dunams of West Bank land, Peace Now reported.

    The Israeli army routinely designates areas as “closed military zones” to forbid Palestinian farmers and international activists from accessing their lands. Legally, this means the land is entirely closed to Palestinians unless authorized by the military. Those entering their fields without prior coordination are committing a criminal offence under Israeli law and face potential removal or arrest.

    Sources indicate that community organizers mentioned, though, that coordinating with the military does not always guarantee their security. “For Area C [i.e. areas under full Israeli security control and civil administration], it is completely forbidden to go, even if we do the necessary coordination,” Abu Naim said. “If we get there with the coordination then settlers come, they provoke, attack, call the army and tell them they’re being attacked, so the army comes and clears the area.”.

    Activists said that the military has claimed certain land is a “closed military zone” without providing documentation, to deter farmers and activists from reaching the olive groves. “They came to us and asked us to leave because we are in a closed military zone,” said Matten Kadish-Berner, an Israeli activist and organizer with Protect the Harvest. “When we asked them to show us the order, they refused, and in the end, they left because they did not have any document.”.

    The Israeli military told Human Rights Watch that the designation of closed military zones is intended to “prevent friction and public order disturbances,” noting that this year, “ahead of the harvest, a dedicated harvest situation room was established for the first time in the Civil Administration.”.

    Israeli authorities routinely intimidate and arrest Palestinians and deport international activists engaged in organizing protection for Palestinian farmers during olive harvest season.

    According to recent reports, on October 27, Israeli soldiers raided Burin village, south of Nablus, and detained about 60 people, noted the Sumood Network, a Palestinian grassroots organization. All were released except Ghassan Najjar, a farmer and rights defender who co-founded the Sumood Network.

    The Sumood Network said that before the season began, security agents from the Shin Bet threatened to detain Najjar if he continued to coordinate protection for the olive harvest in the Nablus area.

    On November 17, an Israeli judge approved a four-month administrative detention order for Najjar, the Sumood Network remarked. During the judicial review, the Israeli Military Prosecution acknowledged that the administrative detention of Najjar is related to political activities that are unarmed and nonviolent, the Sumood Network said. The Israeli military said Najjar “is suspected of hurling stones at Israeli civilians,” which the Sumood Network disputed.

    According to recent reports, israeli authorities often detain Palestinians on the basis of secret evidence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer can see. Orders last up to six months and can be renewed repeatedly, with no limit. International law allows detention without trial only as an exceptional measure, for imperative security reasons, with impartial judicial review. When it is used routinely, it becomes a tool of punishment and control and therefore arbitrary and unlawful.

    According to the Israeli organization HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 Palestinians in administrative detention as of October.

    Recent findings suggest that on October 21, the military detained about 80 US, Israeli, and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including now US Congressman-elect Brad Lander, several rabbis, and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. A few days earlier, Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian, and Polish diplomats, Catholic clergymen, and a French mayor.

    Israeli authorities should release all those held unlawfully under administrative detention, end the systematic use of administrative detention, and ensure Palestinian farmers can safely reach their land.

    Other countries should act to prevent further atrocities across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including by imposing targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing grave abuses, suspending arms transfers to Israel, banning trade with illegal settlements, considering suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel, and supporting the International Criminal Court and its ongoing investigations, including by executing its arrest warrants.

    “Organizing an olive harvest is not a crime,” Sanbar remarked. “Israeli authorities should end their repression of activists and instead fulfill their obligations to protect the Palestinian population.”.

    French Bill Risks Deepening Police Impunity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.
    • The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.
    • Recent findings suggest that because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    Recent findings suggest that because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    The use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    The Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    Sources indicate that if the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    #148510. Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1550 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause.
    • Industry observers note that much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality.
    • Industry observers note that perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause. I've yet to read any actual substantive disagreements with the merits. Rather, there have been a smattering of warnings about the potential consequences of the decision, attacks on the Fifth Circuit's track record in past cases, and predictive judgments about what the Supreme Court will do. I assure you. If you actually read the Fifth Circuit's decision and the dissent, there is not even a close call. Unless consequentialism matters more than originalism.

    Industry observers note that much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality. In order for anyone to challenge a federal statute passed during this period, they would need to have both a reason and standing. Litigation is expensive and time-consuming. Parties do not simply file lawsuits for principle. Again, any remedy would be targeted to a particular law, so it is not possible to wipe out all legislation from this period. The courts do not have a magic eraser for the U.S. Code. Moreover, spending bills and related laws generally do not inflict injuries, so there is no obvious way to challenge many of the bills. Remember that Judge Hendrix found that Texas lacked standing to challenge the DHS Pilot Program, another proxy-passed-statute.

    Industry observers note that perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act. The validity of this statute would only arise in the case of a contested election. There is good reason to have the validity of this law settled. But there is an easy path forward. This was a bipartisan statute that could be re-enacted to eliminate any doubts.

    Recent findings suggest that you might say it is unfair to make Congress re-enact a bill it already passed. I have zero sympathy for the House, which passed a landmark piece of legislation in the face of serious constitutional doubts. There was no actual health emergency that required the rule. The House could have easily followed social distancing protocols to allow members to spread out. The gallery upstairs would serve that purpose well.

    Industry observers note that the House also could have opened a Zoom link for those who are unable to attend. Had these members been able to watch and participate in the proceedings and cast their vote at the time of the roll call, the legal issue would have been much closer. In February 2021, I participated as a virtual witness for Merrick Garland's confirmation hearing. It could be done. Senators who were in the chamber posed questions that I was able to answer.

    In a recent development, the purpose of a deliberative body is to allow members to vote after open deliberation. Designating a vote in advance of the proceeding eliminates any chance for deliberation. Even in my own world, I often walk into a faculty meeting thinking I'll vote one way on a matter, but after hearing other views, I change my position.

    It has been revealed that I suspect others can relate. The Supreme Court satisfied its statutory quorum requirement through remote oral argument. No one would have thought that Chief Justice Roberts could have sat alone in the Chamber, posing the questions that his colleagues sent in advance. Absent Justices could not submit signed proxy votes in advance of the oral argument that would be read aloud at conference. The same rules ought to apply to Congress.

    Industry observers note that the truth is the proxy rule was more about Speaker Pelosi's power than actual pandemic relief. As I said, I have no sympathy when Congress takes shortcuts. Courts with jurisdiction have an unflagging duty to exercise it. And all of the usual presumptions in favor of democracy do not apply when the legislative body ignores the bright-line procedural rules in the constitution. If INS v. Chadha was right--even though the heavens fell--then the quorum case is even righter.

    It has been revealed that what matters to me are originalist principles. And the good judges of the Fifth Circuit followed the law where it leads. They were not cowed by potential consequences in other cases and the predictable hackles from commentators.

    I've started to give the issue a bit more thought, and researched past instances in American history where Congress somehow managed to legislate during times of actual crisis. Here are four highlights.

    Sources indicate that in August 1793, a yellow fever epidemic began to spread through Philadelphia—then the capital of the United States. At the time, Congress was in recess, and it was believed that holding meetings in the capital, including meetings of the legislature, would be unsafe. For that reason, President George Washington asked both James Madison and Thomas Jefferson whether he could summon—in effect, order—Congress to meet in a different location. They both advised that the President lacked the power to change the location of the meeting, but they proposed alternatives. Madison advised that Washington could suggest that the members meet him in nearby Lancaster or Reading, Pennsylvania. Jefferson insisted that Congress "must meet in Philadelphia, "even if it be in the open fields, to adjourn themselves to some other place." I am not aware of any evidence that either Jefferson or Madison or any of their peers ever considered the possibility that the Constitution's quorum rule could be relaxed in order to allow members to establish their presence or otherwise participate by proxy.

    On August 8, 1814, about two weeks before the British would invade Washington, the national capital, and then burn the Capitol, President James Madison called on Congress to convene on September 19. Congress, unwilling to be defeated, found temporary accommodations in the Patent and Post Office Building (now the site of the National Portrait Gallery). Despite the risks of public safety, nearly 90% of the representatives were present. Again, there were no efforts to relax the Constitution's quorum rule, and there were no attempts to facilitate proxies as a means of carrying on legislative business.

    During the American Civil War, debates about the quorum proved particularly vexing by 1864. Should Representatives and Senators from States that took action to join the (purported) Confederate States of America be counted for purposes of a quorum? Ultimately, Senators from the Union States adopted a rule such that quorum was defined as "a majority of the Senators duly chosen." Because the southern state legislatures had not chosen new Senators for the United States Congress, vacancies for authorized senate seats were not filled, and so no one was "duly chosen." Thus, such authorized seats did not count for purposes of the quorum. I do not believe that this rule was an innovation, much less a relaxation of the quorum rule. Rather, the Senate's rule merely clarified the constitutional text and was entirely consistent with prior practice going back to 1790, when the Second Session of the Senate of the First Congress met. Moreover, the Civil War era congresses did not introduce any form of proxy voting.

    In 1918, the Spanish influenza raged through the United States. It is understood that more than one-half million people in the United States would die from this epidemic. The Senate had passed a resolution to authorize the President to appoint certain medical professionals to the Public Health Service. The House, however, lacked a quorum to act, and the Speaker adjourned that day's meeting. The following day, the members worked out a one-time "gentleman's agreement" where no one would object to the lack of a quorum; absent a timely objection by a member in attendance the chair would presume the presence of a quorum. The bill passed under these somewhat unusual parliamentary circumstances, which the House would not repeat during the remainder of the epidemic. There was no attempt to allow absent members to designate a proxy to vote for them. Moreover, the constitutionality of this practice was never tested in court. I agree with Judge Hendrix's take on the Spanish Influenza incident:.

    This occurrence does not support an argument that the Quorum Clause does not require physical presence. Quite the opposite, the House was aware it lacked a quorum at the time, with members urging those who considered raising points of no quorum to withdraw their points because they knew a quorum call would reveal the obvious—the House lacked the physical presence of a quorum and therefore could not proceed to business. And the members sought to pass the bill by unanimous consent because a roll-call vote would reveal the absence of a quorum. The House's decision to proceed in knowing violation of a constitutional requirement does not alter the proper interpretation of that Clause—"[p]ast practice does not, by itself, create power." See Medellín v. Texas, 552 U.S. 491, 532 (2008) (alteration in original) (quoting Dames & Moore v. Regan, 453 U.S. 654, 686 (1981)). Instead, it may merely represent action beyond constitutional authority. But given the House's own acknowledgement at the time and the history previously discussed, the historical practice of the House—even when acting without a quorum—demonstrates an understanding that members must be physically present in order to count towards the quorum.

    According to recent reports, I thank Professor Seth Barrett Tillman for his help with this post. Seth's essay on the Quorum Clause for the Heritage Guide to the Constitution is well worth reading.
